explanations.explanation: Verse 3 says they sent for Jeroboam, and he and the whole assembly of Israel came to Rehoboam. Jeroboam son of Nebat had been living in Egypt, and now he's walking in with the whole crowd. That's a long way from Egypt to the front of the line, baker. Keep your eyes on this guy.

The text says the opposite, friend. “So they sent for Jeroboam, and he and the whole assembly of Israel came to Rehoboam…” (1 Kings 12:3). Jeroboam son of Nebat had been in Egypt, and he doesn't skip this meeting. He shows up, and the whole assembly of Israel comes with him.

That's what they ask, baker. They tell Rehoboam to lighten the burden of his father's service and the heavy yoke Solomon put on them. They don't ask for a party or a parade, just a lighter load. Anybody who's carried too many grocery bags in one trip knows exactly where they're coming from.

Not yet, friend. They came to Shechem to make Rehoboam king (1 Kings 12:1). What they ask him is to lighten the burden of his father's service and the heavy yoke. A king of their own doesn't come up until later in the passage.

Shechem is where they gather, but nobody mentions moving a throne. The text says all Israel went there to make Rehoboam king. Their request is about the yoke Solomon put on them: lighten it, and they will serve him. Furniture never comes up, baker.
They put it right in their request. Lighten the burden and the heavy yoke, “…and we will serve you.” That's a pretty fair deal, friend. The people hand Rehoboam the way to keep them.

Check verse 4 again, baker. The people say, “But now you must lighten the burden of your father’s service and the heavy yoke he put on us, and we will serve you.” So the offer is on the table: a lighter yoke, and they serve him. It's a simple trade.

explanations.answer: Serve the people and speak kindly
explanations.explanation: That's the elders' advice. They tell Rehoboam, “If you will be a servant to these people and serve them this day, and if you will respond by speaking kind words to them, they will be your servants forever.” These men served Solomon during his lifetime. I think that's why their words carry weight, baker.

explanations.answer: Wait until the people calm down
explanations.explanation: The waiting was Rehoboam's own idea. He's the one who told the people to go away for three days. The elders don't tell him to sit tight. They tell him to serve the people this day and speak kind words to them.

Jeroboam is on the other side of this conversation, friend. He's the one who came with the whole assembly to speak to Rehoboam. The elders never mention him. Their advice is that the king himself should be a servant to the people and speak kind words.

That's the word, baker. The elders say, “If you will be a servant to these people and serve them this day, and if you will respond by speaking kind words to them, they will be your servants forever.” (1 Kings 12:7). So the advice is to serve them AND speak kindly. Think about that offer. Some folks can't get a houseplant to stick around that long.
Not quite, friend. The elders promise a lot more than that. They say, “…they will be your servants forever.” It's a long-term deal, not a short one.

Harvest never comes up in these verses, baker. The elders tell Rehoboam that if he will be a servant to the people, serve them this day and speak kind words, “…they will be your servants forever.” No end date on that one. It's a big promise.

Close, but verse 8 says it plainly: “But Rehoboam rejected the advice of the elders…” He asked them, and then he set their answer aside. So the elders' advice goes in the bin, friend. Hang on to that, because it matters for what comes next.

Right, baker. Verse 8 says Rehoboam rejected the advice of the elders, and he went and consulted the young men who had grown up with him and served him. He asked the experienced voices, then walked right past them. That's like reading the recipe, then baking something else entirely.

explanations.answer: One that sounds tougher than his father
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The young men tell him to say, “My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist!” They want him to sound tougher than Solomon. And the people came asking for a lighter load, so this goes the other direction.

explanations.answer: One that sounds gentler than his father
explanations.explanation: That was the elders' side of things, baker. They told him to serve the people and speak kind words. The young men go the other way. They want him to say, “My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist!”

explanations.answer: One that asks the people for more time
explanations.explanation: Stalling isn't what the young men suggest, friend. They don't tell him to ask for more time. They give him a bold answer for the people, starting with, “My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist!” The people return after the advice is given.

That's the line, baker. The young men say, “Whereas my father burdened you with a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke.” The people asked for a lighter yoke, and this answer promises a heavier one. That's the opposite of what they came for.
That would've been gentler than what they say, friend. The young men tell him to say, “…I will add to your yoke.” They don't tell him to leave anything alone. They say add to it.

I wish, baker. Breaking the yoke would've been good news for these people. The young men tell Rehoboam to say, “Whereas my father burdened you with a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke.” It's the opposite of breaking it.

explanations.answer: Harshly like the young men advised
explanations.explanation: That's what verse 13 says. “And the king answered the people harshly.” He rejected the advice of the elders and spoke to them as the young men had advised. The people came back for an answer and got the hard one.

explanations.answer: Warmly with a promise of rest
explanations.explanation: That's what the elders had in mind, baker. They wanted kind words. But the text says the king answered the people harshly, and no promise of rest comes anywhere in his words.
Not this time, friend. Jeroboam and all the people returned to Rehoboam, and the king answered them. The text says he answered them harshly. A quiet note passed along isn't what happens here.

Yep. Verse 15 says, “So the king did not listen to the people, and indeed this turn of events was from the LORD…” The writer wants us to know there's more going on than one king's bad choice. Good ear, baker.

The writer says it outright, friend. “So the king did not listen to the people, and indeed this turn of events was from the LORD, to fulfill the word He had spoken to Jeroboam son of Nebat through Ahijah the Shilonite.” So the writer does say it. Go back and read it twice if you need to.

explanations.answer: They want no part in David's house
explanations.explanation: That's their answer. They say, “What portion do we have in David, and what inheritance in the son of Jesse?” and then, “Look now to your own house, O David!” They're done with the house of David. And then they go home.

explanations.answer: They agree to serve him anyway
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite, baker. They had said they'd serve him if he lightened the yoke. He didn't listen, and they answered, “Look now to your own house, O David!” Serving him isn't in the plan anymore.

explanations.answer: They ask for three more days
explanations.explanation: They already waited three days, friend. They came back on the third day, just as the king had said. After he refused to listen, they answered, “To your tents, O Israel!” and the Israelites went home.
Not quite, baker. Verse 17 says, “…but Rehoboam still reigned over the Israelites living in the cities of Judah.” So he lost a lot, but he did not lose everyone. Some Israelites were still under him.

That's right, friend. The Israelites went home, “…but Rehoboam still reigned over the Israelites living in the cities of Judah.” He lost a lot, but he did not lose everyone. He still had a kingdom, just a smaller one.

explanations.answer: He escapes to Jerusalem in his chariot
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says, baker. Rehoboam “…mounted his chariot in haste and escaped to Jerusalem.” In haste means he didn't take his time. I think that chariot got a real workout that day.

explanations.answer: He hides in Shechem with his guards
explanations.explanation: The text sends him somewhere else, friend. After all Israel stoned Adoram, Rehoboam mounted his chariot in haste and escaped to Jerusalem. The passage doesn't say he hides anywhere else, and no guards come up either.

explanations.answer: He calls the elders back for advice
explanations.explanation: I wish he had, baker. But the text never shows him going back to the elders. They gave him their advice, and he rejected it. After Adoram is stoned, he mounts his chariot in haste and escapes to Jerusalem.

That's the word, baker. Verse 20 says, “When all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they summoned him to the assembly and made him king over all Israel.” Jeroboam went from Egypt to wearing the crown. And only the tribe of Judah followed the house of David.

Not this one, friend. Verse 20 says they summoned Jeroboam to the assembly and made him king over all Israel. Judge is a fine title, but it's not the one on the crown. I think Jeroboam wouldn't mind the upgrade from Egypt.
That's a different job, baker. In verse 20, they summon Jeroboam to the assembly and make him king over all Israel. Nobody hands him a priest's role in this passage.

That's it, friend. Rehoboam mobilizes 180,000 chosen warriors “…to fight against the house of Israel and restore the kingdom to Rehoboam son of Solomon.” That's a LOT of warriors. And they're gathered against people who used to be his own.
Egypt is where Jeroboam had been, baker. But he's back now, and the people made him king over all Israel. Rehoboam gathers his warriors to fight against the house of Israel.

Edom doesn't show up in these verses, friend. Rehoboam gathers the whole house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, 180,000 chosen warriors. His target is the house of Israel, because he wants to restore the kingdom to himself.

explanations.answer: Don't fight your brothers and go home
explanations.explanation: That's the message, baker. The LORD says through Shemaiah, “You are not to go up and fight against your brothers, the Israelites. Each of you must return home, for this is My doing.” Rehoboam brought 180,000 warriors, and the answer is to go home. That's a big plan getting a clear no.

explanations.answer: Go up and win the kingdom back
explanations.explanation: That was Rehoboam's plan, friend. He mobilized the warriors to restore the kingdom to himself. But the word of God comes to Shemaiah, a man of God, and says, “You are not to go up and fight against your brothers, the Israelites.” The LORD tells them to stand down.

explanations.answer: Wait three days and then attack
explanations.explanation: Three days already happened earlier, baker. That's when Rehoboam told the people to go away and come back. This time the LORD's word through Shemaiah says, “You are not to go up and fight against your brothers, the Israelites.” No attack at all.
Close, friend, but the ending goes the other way. Verse 24 says, “So they listened to the word of the LORD and turned back according to the word of the LORD.” They did not march out. They went home.

That's right, baker. The passage ends with, “So they listened to the word of the LORD and turned back according to the word of the LORD.” 180,000 warriors hear the LORD say to go home, and they go home. That's a whole army turning around.
